refer.label: Electrical panel or service
refer.why: Panel and service work needs a permit and a licensed electrician in most places.

sources.says: A building permit is required for panel replacement or adding a sub-panel, and for electrical service upgrades.
It is illegal for an unlicensed person to work on any project which requires a building permit.

refer.label: New wiring or moved outlets
refer.why: New wiring, new circuits and moved outlets change the electrical system: a permit and a licensed electrician in most places.

sources.says: A building permit is required for any changes to the electrical, gas, mechanical or plumbing systems, including relocating electrical receptacles.
Simple fixture replacements can be handled by experienced handypersons, while new wiring requires a licensed electrician.

refer.trade: a licensed plumber or gas fitter
refer.label: Gas lines or gas appliances
refer.why: Gas lines, gas appliances and gas logs need a permit and a licensed pro in most places.

sources.says: A building permit is required for any changes to the gas system and for fireplace or gas log installation.
Installation, repair or replacement of a residential gas appliance or a combustion system on a small project shall be performed by a person certified under 58-55-308(2).

refer.label: Water heater
refer.why: Water heaters need a permit in most places, and Florida lists replacing one as licensed work.

sources.says: A building permit is required for water heaters.

sources.publisher: Florida DBPR guidance, posted by Columbia County
sources.says: Replacing a water heater for pay requires a state license.

refer.label: Moving or adding pipes, drains or valves
refer.why: Moving or adding pipes, drains and valves changes the plumbing system: a permit and a licensed plumber in most places.

sources.says: A building permit is required for any changes to the plumbing system.
If the project calls for moving supply lines, changing valves or drilling new sink holes, bring in a licensed plumber.
Permit-free plumbing is limited to faucet or toilet repair or replacement, stopping leaks and clearing stoppages without replacing valves or pipes.

refer.label: Heating or cooling system
refer.why: Heating and cooling systems need a licensed HVAC pro in most places: Utah's rule says so even on small jobs, and Florida lists central air as licensed work.

sources.says: Installation, repair or replacement of a heating, ventilation or air conditioning system on a small project must be performed by an HVAC contractor licensed by the division.

sources.publisher: Florida DBPR guidance, posted by Columbia County
sources.says: Installing central air conditioning for pay requires a state license; changing an AC filter or setting up a plug-in window unit does not.

refer.label: Structural work
refer.why: Structural work (load-bearing walls, beams, joists, foundations and new openings) needs a permit and a licensed contractor in most places.

sources.says: A building permit is required for any repairs involving structural members.

sources.publisher: Florida DBPR guidance, posted by Columbia County
sources.says: Structural alterations to load-bearing walls for pay require a state contractor's license.
Ordinary repairs do not include cutting away a wall, or removing a beam or load-bearing support.

electrical_swap.label: Light, fan, outlet or switch swap
electrical_swap.say: Swapping a fixture, fan, outlet or switch in an existing box needs no permit in some cities (Cotati lists them), but some states require a licensed electrician even for a swap.

plumbing_swap.label: Faucet, toilet or disposal swap
plumbing_swap.say: Swapping a faucet or toilet in the same spot needs no permit in some cities (Cotati lists them), but some states require a licensed plumber even for a swap.

plumbing_fix.label: Small plumbing repair
plumbing_fix.say: Repairs that don't replace pipes or valves, like a flapper or a clog, need no permit in some cities (Cotati), but some states still require a licensed plumber.

hvac_swap.label: Thermostat swap
hvac_swap.say: Some states treat any heating and cooling work as licensed work.

door_window.label: Door or window replacement
door_window.say: A same-size door or window swap needs no permit in some cities (Cotati), but some cities require one; a new or bigger opening is structural work.

roof.label: Roof repair
roof.say: Roofing is licensed work in some states (Florida lists it), and cities set when a roof repair needs a permit.

appliance.label: Appliance hookup
appliance.say: Connecting a dishwasher or an ice maker to the water line counts as plumbing in some states (Florida lists a dishwasher connected to drinking water as licensed work).

check_sources.says: Work exempt from a permit includes light fixture or ceiling fan replacement, outlet and switch replacements in existing boxes, faucet or toilet repair or replacement, stopping leaks, clearing stoppages without replacing valves or pipes, and window replacements that don't alter the frame.

check_sources.publisher: Florida DBPR guidance, posted by Columbia County
check_sources.says: Licensed work includes connecting a dishwasher to drinking water, replacing a water heater, central air conditioning, plumbing that connects to drinking water, roofing and load-bearing walls; painting, cabinets and drywall without plumbing, electrical or AC work need no state license.

CA.name: California
CA.rule: California: without a contractor license you can take a job only if labor and materials together come to less than $1,000, no building permit is needed and you employ no one for it. Ads for this work must say you are not licensed.

sources.says: Starting January 1, 2025, AB 2622 raises the minor work license exemption from $500 to $1,000, but the work cannot require a permit and the unlicensed person cannot employ anyone; unlicensed individuals can advertise for work up to $1,000 if the ad says they are not licensed.
A license is needed for work of $1,000 or more in combined labor and material costs, and it is illegal for an unlicensed person to work on any project which requires a building permit.

notes: Cities such as Cotati list light fixture, fan, outlet and switch swaps and faucet and toilet repairs or replacements as work that needs no permit. Check your city.
CA.banner: California: an unlicensed handyperson's ads must say they are not licensed (CSLB).

AZ.name: Arizona
AZ.rule: Arizona: the handyman exemption covers one job under $1,000 in labor, materials and everything else, of a casual or minor nature, with no local building permit. It doesn't cover work split into smaller contracts or part of a larger job, and ads must say "not a licensed contractor".

sources.says: Exempt: work on one undertaking or project by one or more contracts with an aggregate contract price, including labor, materials and all other items, of less than $1,000, of a casual or minor nature; not if the work requires a local building permit, is part of a larger operation or split to evade the chapter, or if the person's ads don't include the words "not a licensed contractor".

AZ.banner: Arizona: put "not a licensed contractor" on your ads, cards and door hangers while you work under the exemption (A.R.S. 32-1121).

NV.name: Nevada
NV.rule: Nevada: repair or upkeep under $1,000 in labor and materials is exempt, unless it needs a building permit, is work a plumbing, electrical, refrigeration, heating or air-conditioning contractor does, or is part of a larger project of $500 or more.

sources.says: NRS 624.031(6): any work to repair or maintain property the value of which is less than $1,000, including labor and materials, is exempt unless a building permit is required, the work is of a type performed by a plumbing, electrical, refrigeration, heating or air-conditioning contractor, or it is part of a larger project of $500 or more or split to evade the chapter.

OR.name: Oregon
OR.rule: Oregon: a handyman needs a CCB license for any job of $1,000 or more, and for any job at all once they advertise, even with business cards.

sources.says: Any handyman that performs work of $1,000 or more must be licensed by the CCB; handymen must also be licensed if they produce any form of advertisements, including business cards. A lead-based paint license is required to bid and work on pre-1978 homes.

ORS 701.010(4): the exemption for casual, minor or inconsequential work under $1,000 does not apply to a person who advertises or puts out any sign or card or other device that might indicate to the public that the person is a contractor.

OR.banner: Oregon: handymen who advertise, even with business cards, must be licensed by the CCB. Get your CCB license before you hand out cards or quote this list.
OR.lead: Oregon also requires a CCB lead-based paint license to bid and work on homes built before 1978.

UT.name: Utah
UT.rule: Utah: alteration or repair under $7,000 in labor and materials is exempt, but plumbing and electrical work goes to a licensed contractor, or a licensed journeyman for parts like a faucet, toilet, fixture, outlet or switch; heating and cooling systems to a licensed HVAC contractor; gas appliances to a certified person.

sources.says: 58-55-305(1)(h): alteration or repair of a building with a contracted value of less than $7,000, including labor and materials, is exempt; plumbing and electrical work must be done by a licensed electrical or plumbing contractor, or by a licensed journeyman for a component such as a faucet, toilet, fixture, device, outlet or electrical switch; HVAC work by a licensed HVAC contractor; above $3,000 the person files a one-time affirmation of liability insurance. (1)(k): minor plumbing incidental to the repair of a fixture or appliance is exempt if no piping or gas appliance is modified.

notes: Utah: a small plumbing repair to a fixture, with no change to the pipes or a gas appliance, is exempt (58-55-305(1)(k)).
UT.over: Utah: on a job over $3,000 you file a one-time affirmation with the state that you carry liability insurance (58-55-305(1)(h)).

FL.name: Florida
FL.rule: Florida: the minor-work exemption covers jobs under $2,500 in labor, materials and everything else, of a casual, minor or inconsequential nature, not part of a larger job or split into smaller contracts, and not for anyone who advertises as a contractor. Electrical work for pay has no such exemption.

sources.says: 489.103(9) (2026): the exemption covers work of a casual, minor or inconsequential nature with an aggregate contract price for labor, materials and all other items under $2,500; not for work that is part of a larger or major operation or divided into smaller contracts, and not for a person who advertises as a contractor.
489.503 (2026) has no exemption for unlicensed persons doing minor electrical work for pay.

sources.publisher: Florida DBPR guidance, posted by Columbia County
sources.says: Licensed work includes connecting a dishwasher to drinking water, replacing a water heater, plumbing that connects to drinking water, central air conditioning, roofing and load-bearing walls; check your county or city for local licensing too.

notes: Florida: many counties and cities also have their own license rules. Check yours.

VA.name: Virginia
VA.rule: Virginia: a Class C contractor license is needed for a single contract or project over $1,000 (up to $30,000), and electrical, plumbing and HVAC contractors need a master tradesman license.

sources.says: Class C contractors perform or manage construction, removal, repair or improvements when the total value of a single contract or project is over $1,000 but less than $30,000; the Board requires a master tradesman license for electrical, plumbing and HVAC contractors.

default_state.rule: This pack doesn't have your state's rule yet. Some states cap the size of a job you can take without a contractor license, and the cap differs by state. Check your state's contractor licensing board and your city's building department before you quote.

sources.says: Some states cap the dollar value of jobs you can take without a contractor license ($500 to $10,000 or more, depending on the state); if the job crosses into licensed trade work, refer it out or partner with a licensed pro.

lead.always: Window replacement always counts under EPA's lead rule (RRP) in a home built before 1978, whatever the size.
lead.area: In a home built before 1978, EPA's lead rule (RRP) covers paid work that disturbs more than 6 square feet of paint in a room, or more than 20 square feet outside: you need an EPA- or state-certified firm and a certified renovator, even as a one-person business.
lead.ask: Ask what year the home was built.

sources.says: Jobs that disturb six square feet or less of paint per room inside, or 20 square feet or less on the exterior, are not covered; window replacement and demolition of painted surfaces are always covered; this includes all firms, even sole proprietorships.

Minor repair and maintenance activities, including minor electrical work and plumbing, disrupt 6 square feet or less of painted surface per room inside or 20 square feet or less outside, and do not involve window replacement or demolition of painted surfaces.

materials.say: Small hardware like screws and anchors is in the price. Bigger parts are extra: the customer buys them, or you buy them and bill them with the receipt.

sources.says: Build small hardware like screws, anchors and nails into your hourly rate; bill separately for parts that cost real money, like a replacement faucet cartridge or fan motor.
Customers can provide materials themselves, or the handyman may supply them with a 10 to 30% markup.

estimate.hourly: Billed by the hour at {rate} an hour, with a trip minimum of {minimum}.
estimate.scope: If I find hidden damage or the job grows, I explain the options and ask before doing any extra work.

sources.says: Suggested estimate language: if we find hidden damage or the scope changes, I'll explain the options before doing extra work. Put change orders in writing before adding scope.
For a full punch list, estimate your total hours, apply your hourly rate, add materials, then quote a flat project price.
Handymen who charge an hourly rate will often have a minimum charge: even if the task takes 20 minutes, you are likely to be charged for a full hour. Group together smaller household jobs.

estimate.visits_note: Visits of up to 8 hours each, a judgment call.
estimate.order_note: The order is a judgment call, except patches first so they can dry (TaskRabbit).
estimate.math: Each job's time comes from the sources in its line (or a judgment call, marked). The price is the middle of the time range at your hourly rate, the way Housecall Pro prices a full punch list, with the trip minimum. Each job's typical price alone, where two or more guides give one, is shown to you for comparison, never on the estimate.

ladder.label: Ladder work
ladder.say: Set the foot about a quarter of the ladder's length out from the wall, extend it 3 feet above the landing, never stand on a stepladder's top step, and use a nonconductive ladder near live wires (OSHA 1926.1053).

sources.says: Portable ladders used to reach an upper landing extend at least 3 feet above it; a non-self-supporting ladder is set so the foot is about one-quarter of the working length out from the top support; the top step of a stepladder is not used as a step; ladders near exposed energized electrical equipment have nonconductive side rails.

anchor.label: Tip-overs
anchor.say: Anchor TVs, dressers and bookcases securely to the wall (CPSC).

sources.says: Anchor TVs and furniture like bookcases and dressers securely to the wall.
